Share The Hormuz bonus: Sailor salaries soar for transits amid Iran war on social media
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on October 6, 2026 [Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters]
As shipping traffic through the besieged Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level since July this week, reports have emerged that sailors are being paid large bonuses for making the dangerous trip through the Gulf waterway.
Some captains are earning base salaries of as much as $100,000 – the high end of usual salaries which vary greatly between shipping companies – plus a $50,000 bonus per voyage through the strait, the UK’s Financial Times has reported.

list 2 of 3 What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure?
list 3 of 3 US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
Oil exports from the Middle East rose above pre-war levels at the end of last month despite ongoing attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. But shipping data from Kpler shows that about 40 percent of those are leaving the region due to a combination of pipeline exports and small shuttle boats carrying out risky ship-to-ship transfers.
Yes. According to shipping data from Kpler, at least 16.5 million barrels left the region last month, matching the pre-war average, excluding Iran, which is under a naval blockade by the United States.
However, about 40 percent of this is being exported via Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline or via ship-to-ship transfers by smaller boats travelling undetected through the strait.
Kpler reported on Tuesday that the number of detectable vessels passing through the strait had fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, with only seven vessels passing through the crucial waterway in the previous week, the lowest figure since July 23.
Data is hard to determine, as many smaller shuttle boats are turning off their transponders to avoid detection when travelling through the strait before offloading oil to larger tankers waiting beyond it.
[Al Jazeera] How dangerous is it for sailors in the strait?
Very. Attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued in the past week.
On Wednesday night, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several casualties after multiple projectiles struck a vessel sailing off Qatar’s northern coast.
Following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February, Tehran all but closed the strait, with limited vessels receiving clearance. Iran has launched strikes at ships making the crossing without its express permission.
The US, for its part, imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports due to Tehran’s closure and has escorted some vessels through the waterway.
Last week, attacks on tankers in the strait hit their highest level since the war began as regional oil producers tried to increase exports at heightened risk for crew and cargo.
Saul Kavonic, energy head at MST Marquee, told the Reuters news agency: “The frequency of Iranian attacks on ships is now at the highest point since the war began, and likely to intensify further.”
He added that “constrained product flows, extreme logistics costs and high likelihood of Iranian escalation are keeping [oil] prices elevated”.
Mohamed El Hawawy, head of Middle East shipping and insurance at international law firm Stephenson Harwood, said: “I guess more attacks will make more [shipping companies] reluctant to pass the strait, which will perhaps affect trade.”
“It could be more costly on the insurance and other associated costs with transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” he added.
Oil prices rose on Thursday morning, with Brent crude futures increasing by $2.28, or 2.28 percent, to $102.28 a barrel by 04:27 GMT.
US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88 percent, to $89.94.
This is despite oil exports recovering to some extent due to Saudi Arabia using alternative export infrastructure and due to the complex system of ship-to-ship transfers.
The East-West pipeline , which carries oil from fields in Saudi Arabia’s east to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea in the west, has been crucial to this process. However, it has also come under threat and been forced to close at times due to strikes from Iran-backed groups.
(Al Jazeera) What incentives are sailors receiving for crossing the strait?
The Financial Times reported this week that tanker captains can now command a base salary of $100,000, plus a $50,000 per-trip bonus, to make the dangerous transit.
Overall, the crew on board each ship can earn four to six times their normal salaries.
On Monday, The Wall Street Journal reported that shipping companies were spending between $30m and $40m for a single round trip to move oil in and out of Hormuz through ship-to-ship transfers.
It added that oil producers now have to swallow high costs to get oil out of the waterway, with shipowners and individual sailors making some of the best returns the industry has seen in decades. Many sailors willing to risk the trip are coming from India, the Philippines and China to do so.
“One Shandong-based ship-staffing company is even offering as much as $25,000 for a round trip as reward, according to seafarers and recruitment advertisements seen by The Wall Street Journal. For oilers and cadets [low-level crewmembers of a commercial ship] the $25,000 could represent more than a year of wages,” the outlet reported.
El Hawawy explained that the higher captain salaries are part of a “new economics” in crossing the waterway, adding that shipping cannot just stop.
“So far I don’t see a reason for it not to be sustainable, and actually that’s something will happen beyond the cost,” he said.
As with the smaller shuttle boats that move in and out of the strait under threat of attack, captains on board larger ships and tankers must turn off their lights and transponders to make the journey.
According to Bloomberg, which spoke to a captain on a vessel that was part of the shuttle runs, his vessel, which frequently carries barrels at night, is given strict instructions: no lights, no phones, and only one radar on as they cross.
Speaking from the Philippines, where he has arrived following a three-month stint taking vessels through the strait, he explained that he and his crew got their bearings by using the coast and lighthouses as a reference, adding that it is “quite challenging”.
After seeing a fire ahead on one trip, the captain said he called the US Navy, which has been assisting ships on routes through the waterway to avoid mines, to warn them of an attack.
He added that his most recent contract through the strait was shorter than usual since he knew the voyage was “not easy”, but he still received several times his usual salary for the trip.
Another captain of a Liquefied Natural Gas tanker told Bloomberg that his journey began by turning off the breaker that connects the ship’s location transponder to hide their whereabouts while they were travelling along the Omani coast.
Crew members also barricade the main decks with sandbags in case drones or missiles attack them.
The report added that shipping executives estimate a one-in-20 chance of being hit while crossing the strait at present.

items.title: Europe stocks retreat after three-day rise as rising yields, oil dent sentiment - Reuters
items.summary: Europe stocks retreat after three-day rise as rising yields, oil dent sentiment  Reuters
items.content:
Image caption, Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the start of the Iran war (file photo)
By David Gritten   and   Joshua Cheetham ,  BBC Verify
A tanker has been struck by "multiple projectiles" north of Qatar in the Gulf, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
The incident - a rare attack deep inside the Gulf - happened 51 nautical miles (94km) from Madinat al-Shamal with casualties reported, the UKMTO said.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel as the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers. On Saturday it was reported as sailing towards the Strait of Hormuz waterway, which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman.
Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the region since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.
At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 93 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization (IMO).
The IMO said the last incident that resulted in casualties was on 9 September, when two sailors were killed in an attack on the Panama-flagged tanker El Gaia in the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Oman's Musandam peninsula.
This is also the first reported attack on a ship this far west of the Strait of Hormuz since that same day, according to Martin Kelly, head of advisory at EOS Risk Group.
Also on Thursday, Vanguard amended an earlier report that had said there was a fire on board another tanker in the Gulf of Oman, about 40km east of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
The company clarified that there were no indications a fire occurred on the vessel, which it had identified as the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalkut.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Tehran's missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Over the past two weeks, crude exports through the waterway have averaged 12 million barrels per day (bpd), which is around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler.

Tanker attacked off Qatar as Iran claims route transporting oil through strait of Hormuz will be ‘closed’

A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties, a British maritime security agency said. The attack came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic.
The vessel was in the Gulf, about 500km (300 miles) west of the strait of Hormuz, when it reported being struck “by multiple projectiles”, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Wednesday. The UK authority did not specify the origin of the ship.
Wednesday’s attack comes as strikes on tankers sailing through the strait of Hormuz hit their ⁠highest weekly level since the Iran war began, according to maritime security firms, as oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel.

In the ‌week to 5 October, there were at least 12 attacks ‌on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait, according to data from three security sources.
On Tuesday, India’s ​foreign ministry said 12 crew members were injured after an attack on a Panama-flagged oil tanker passing through the strait of Hormuz.
Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights and surveillanceby Iran’s Revolutionary ⁠Guards have persisted in the strait, a US Navy-led agency said on Sunday.
“These actions ⁠continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes ​and maintain pressure on transiting vessels,” ‌the Joint Maritime Information Center said.
Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait, the only way in or out of the oil-rich region for vessels, have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
On Wednesday, Tehran said it would further choke Hormuz, declaring transit routes in the strait deemed illegal by Iran ⁠would soon be closed, in reference to a southern pathway hugging Oman’s coast.
Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, said these “few routes” had been created by blasting and damaging ⁠some of the rocky passages and were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring ⁠it to tankers”, despite evidence Gulf oil exports are regaining ​prewar levels .
“The strait of ‌Hormuz is closed, ‌and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have ‌full control over it,” he told the Fars news agency.
Graphic The IRGC has consistently denied that seaborne crude flows in the strait are rebounding thanks to US Navy help. IRGC adviser Majid Mirahmadi said on ⁠Thursday that a daily average of 10 ships were transiting the ​waterway against ​an average of 125 before the ​war.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, disputed that account on Wednesday, saying Iran had “lost complete control” of the strait. “There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began.”
Amid mixed messaging and supply concerns, the price of oil rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude topping $100 per barrel.
The continuing stalemate in the war is heaping pressure on Donald Trump. The US president is reportedly considering resuming military operations against Iran in the coming weeks, including the option of launching strikes before November’s midterm elections, according to reports in US media.
Last week, a third US aircraft carrier set sail for the region . It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October.
Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
As a result of Trump’s war with Iran, Americans have been grappling with high gas prices and soaring diesel costs .
The US has set up its own counter blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran. It has also bombed Iranian targets in retaliation for Tehran’s attacks on ships, although there have been no such reported strikes since 1 September.
Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began.

items.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  AP News
items.content:
Federal Reserve officials expect another rate hike will be needed this year, according to minutes
Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting showed
WASHINGTON -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank's most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries , gas and housing , and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.

Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed's rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month's rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.

items.title: 'Every day there is killing': Palestinians in Gaza face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
items.summary: Many Palestinians are still living in cramped tent cities, with the US plan to end the war largely stalled.
items.content:
Figure caption, Fida al-Toutah's family say they witnessed her being killed by Israeli gunfire in their tent two weeks ago
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Image caption, Fida was one of the more than 1,400 people killed since the ceasefire began, according to Gaza's health ministry
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Image caption, Ibrahim has lost four siblings, including Fida, since the start of the war in 2023
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Image caption, Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza a year after a ceasefire came into force
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
Image caption, Amal Alabadla says she's struggling to raise her sons alone inside a tent on Gaza's coast
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."

items.content:
Image caption, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv's allies needed to take "concrete action"
By Olivia Ireland   and   Toby Luckhurst ,  in Kyiv
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meeting Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the attack in Pryluky showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Donetsk regional head Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.
Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 22 in block of flats
Civilians told to flee Ukraine's fortress cities as Russia bids to control Donbas
Russia is also launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing throughout the day.
Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko said attacks on Thursday had killed three people, with 14 others injured. Two of the eight injured are in a critical condition.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.

items.title: South Korea recalls ambassador to Ukraine amid dispute with Kyiv - Reuters
items.summary: South Korea recalls ambassador to Ukraine amid dispute with Kyiv  Reuters
items.content:
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia
Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

items.content:
Fed's Waller sees additional rate hikes to get inflation down faster
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation faster if economic data comes in as he expects.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Waller said at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye İstanbul Economic Forum. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Waller noted a convergence of factors have gelled into persistent inflationary forces, including hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict and warnings that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. He also pointed out that the artificial intelligence build-out has significantly driven up high-tech consumer prices , and projections of its size have ballooned. Additionally, he said, continuing trade conflicts threaten new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again.
"When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target," Waller said.
Waller sees economic activity strengthening in the second half of this year, and says he's "not greatly concerned" that higher interest rates threaten to markedly slow down the economy.
"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."
He noted that he sees the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the Fed's policy meeting in mid-September.
"Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high," he said. "For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate."
Waller also made a point of sharing how he believes the Fed should communicate its interest rate expectations . He doesn't think choosing to say nothing or offering a strong indication of what the Fed will do is how the central bank should communicate. Rather, he believes an in-between approach of signaling the amount of rate hikes over some time interval, while not saying what the pace of hikes will be or how large they will be, would offer flexibility, while keeping the public informed.
"We could emphasize that the course of monetary policy is not predetermined and will depend on incoming data," he said.
"Policymakers could signal where they are likely headed while acknowledging that there is no fixed final destination — except for the achievement of price stability and maximum employment."

Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Christa Pike's "shock" recovery in hospital
Christa Pike is "up and walking" though mentally "foggy" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but had learned her arms were swollen and barely functioning as she took her first steps around her hospital room.
A court has ordered state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
How did Christa Pike survive two lethal injections?
In their previous updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.
Her lawyer Randy Spivey said after Wednesday's court hearing: "She cannot move either of her arms." He added: "Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what if any function she will regain in her arms."
In the later updates, given on Wednesday to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital.
The drug was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September. But once it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the execution attempt, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to be in a critical condition.
As of late on Wednesday, though, Pike was "fairly well", Ferrell said.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, Ferrell added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".
Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend
Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.
For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.
The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.
Correction 8 October: This article originally said that Pike and her boyfriend had first met Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp for "troubled teens". This has been amended to make clear that the scheme was for low-income youths aged 16 to 24 and was not specifically for troubled teenagers.

items.title: French students vow to continue protests, saying ministers’ pledges not enough
items.summary: Schools blockaded again across country as teenagers and teachers demand more investment and ‘concrete measures’ to improve conditionsEurope live – latest updatesHigh school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign despite government pled
items.content:
A protester reading a book as teargas is sprayed by police during a blockade near Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Thursday. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
A protester reading a book as teargas is sprayed by police during a blockade near Hélène Boucher high school in Paris on Thursday. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images
French students vow to continue protests, saying ministers’ pledges not enough
Schools blockaded again across country as teenagers and teachers demand more investment and ‘concrete measures’ to improve conditions
High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France , promising to continue their campaign despite government pledges to address the grievances underlying 10 days of protests that have left hundreds injured.
Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a procession marched through the city centre to arrive at the Place de la Bastille.
Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved.
Crowds gathered at the Place de la Bastille on Thursday. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said after meeting students and teachers on Thursday at a school in the eastern city of Reims that he was “implementing an emergency plan to ensure absent teachers can be replaced on a long-term basis”.
Heavy timetables were also under review, Geffray said, as were changes to the widely criticised university application system. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised a “concrete, rapid and fully funded” response by the end of the month.
‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
Students said the government’s reaction was not sufficient. Ryad Rani, president of one high school student’s union, said the protesters had heard “no concrete measures whatsoever, no response to our demands”. The movement “will continue”, he said.
Sabrine Kharbach, from another students’ association, said the protest would last “for as long as €10bn hasn’t been put on the table” – the amount students and some leftwing politicians have said needs to be urgently invested in France’s schools.
According to an Elabe poll ​for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students’ demands are legitimate but 55% of them think the protests should stop. Unions called for another national day of action in support of the students next Tuesday.
Burning bins during a blockade of a school in Toulouse on Thursday. Photograph: Lionel Bonaventure/AFP/Getty Images The education ministry said fewer high schools had been forced to close than in recent days, with 224 shut on Thursday morning and 157 by lunchtime, meaning that about 95% of the county’s high schools were at least partly open.
But several marches drew up to 5,000 protesters, and the demonstrations, backed by many teachers, parents and unions, involved further clashes with police in Paris. In Rennes riot officers used water cannon to disperse protesters.
A prominent complaint on student banners and placards was the heavy-handed police response to the wave of protests. “Too young to be listened ​to, but old enough to be teargassed,” read one banner on the Paris march.
Protesters clashing with French gendarmes in Nantes on Thursday. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters Over the past two weeks, some demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded using batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.
At least 215 teenagers, 89 school staff and 761 police officers had been injured since the start of the protests, which were triggered by chronic teacher shortages, crowded classes, dilapidated buildings and long school days.
The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students | Editorial
The government on Wednesday suspended the use of stun grenades by police after a teenager’s hand was blown off, while saying it was “excessive” to speak of “police repression” and denying that officers had “orders to confront” the young protesters.
The protests have rocked a government caught between popular demands for investments in deteriorating public services and pressure from markets to reduce France’s ballooning budget deficit and debt mountain, among the highest in the EU.
The economy minister, Roland Lescure, said this week there was room to address demands for more school resources in the 2027 budget. In the current draft, schools have the second-largest funding increase after defence, with a 1.4% hike to €90.9bn.
Six months away from a crucial presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, politicians are jockeying to exploit the protests, with the far-right frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, highlighted the damage to schools and called for parents ⁠to foot repair bills.
Her hard-left opponent, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has praised the protesters ​as “incredible” and denounced police brutality.

EU lawmakers vote to reject Chinese pressure on Taiwan's global role

Brussels, Oct. 7 (CNA) The European Parliament on Wednesday adopted a recommendation on European Union (EU)-China political relations that rejected China's efforts to restrict Taiwan's participation in international organizations and exchanges.
The recommendation, addressed to the European Council, the European Commission and the EU foreign policy chief, includes several references to EU-Taiwan relations and expresses support for closer ties, saying they would bring positive benefits and have strategic importance.
Describing Taiwan as a valuable partner in trade and technology, the European Parliament said it "rejects China's attempts to coerce international organizations, third countries and other actors into restricting Taiwan's international participation and contacts."
The recommendation reaffirms that the EU's "One China policy" guides its policy toward Taiwan and stresses that the EU has never endorsed China's "One China principle."
It also opposes any unilateral attempt to change the status quo by force or coercion, or any provocation or any change against the will of the Taiwanese people.
The recommendation calls for the EU and its member states to work with other democratic partners in the region on closer security coordination, including a continuous naval presence and joint exercises, to reinforce regional stability.
It also calls on the European Commission to fulfill its pledge to Parliament to work toward deterring China from provoking or escalating tensions with Taiwan.
At the same time, it says the Commission should continue to develop EU-Taiwan relations in various areas under the EU's longstanding "One China policy" and encourage dialogue and constructive engagement across the Taiwan Strait.
The recommendation also calls on the United Nations to reject Chinese demands and grant Republic of China (Taiwan) passport holders, including tourists, journalists, nongovernmental organization workers and political activists, access to tours and events at the U.N.
The European Parliament also opposes what it describes as China's distortion of U.N. Resolution 2758 to support its claims over Taiwan's territory and sovereignty.
U.N. Resolution 2758 does not mention Taiwan and addresses only the issue of China's U.N. representation. Beijing interprets the resolution as giving it the right to represent Taiwan, which it claims as part of its territory.
The recommendation also stresses the importance of deepening economic and technological cooperation with Taiwan in areas such as semiconductors and cybersecurity to strengthen Europe's resilience and protect critical supply chains.
It calls for the EU to begin preparations without delay for negotiations on a bilateral investment agreement or another arrangement, such as a memorandum of understanding on critical supply chains, with Taiwan.

Share ‘New tactic’: Russia expands deadly attacks on Ukraine’s transport system on social media
Russian glide bomb hits buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk, killing at least 30
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.
Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.

list 2 of 4 Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two
list 3 of 4 At least 24 killed as Russia launches massive attack on Ukraine
list 4 of 4 Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.
Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.
“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”
“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.
“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”
The wreckage of a bus following a Russian missile strike in the eastern city of Kramatorsk, Ukraine [Maria Senovilla/EPA] Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.
With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.
Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.
At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.
Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.
The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.
Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.
“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.
Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.
Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.
The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.
A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.
When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.
She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.
The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.
The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.
“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.
Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.
The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.
“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.
Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets , and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

China's real estate market may be set for a turnaround, S&P says
China's real estate market is nearing a bottom, S&P Global Ratings said, based on a comparison to how housing crises in other countries played out.
Two of Beijing's recent measures to support real estate are also at play, S&P's Edward Chan said.
The largest Chinese cities could see a glimmer of property market recovery as soon as this quarter, Guotai Junan International said.
A real estate project under construction in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China, on September 15, 2026.
BEIJING — An end is in sight for China's yearslong property market slump, S&P Global Ratings analysts said in a report distributed Thursday.
Residential real estate prices may hit a bottom in the third quarter of 2028, the report said. It added that prices in China's largest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, will likely recover as soon as next year.
That's a big shift from February, when S&P said high levels of unsold housing kept "a property market recovery out of reach ."
What's changed since are two government policies, according to the report's author Edward Chan, a credit analyst at S&P Global Ratings.
In August, Beijing announced new restrictions on developers' ability to sell unfinished properties. A month later, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the government would roll out policies for stabilizing the real estate sector . Beijing subsequently launched a mortgage rate subsidy for first-time homebuyers of units less than 1.5 million yuan ($220,000) and smaller than 120 square meters (1291.67 square feet).
"Developers will now be very cautious in buying land, so they will basically buy less land and develop less new projects going forward," Chan said in a phone interview with CNBC on Thursday. "That may not be good for the revenue but that will help China's oversupplied property market."
"Going forward in the next one to two years, the major factor in helping stabilize China's home price is the continued reduction of supply," he said, noting that despite a multi-year property slump, 2026 is the first year of real estate inventory destocking.
The oversupply challenge was so big that in 2023, Nomura estimated the scale of unfinished, pre-sold homes in China was about 20 times the size of Country Garden , as of the end of 2022. Country Garden was once the largest non-state-owned developer in China by sales.
Chinese property developers such as Evergrande long relied on sales of apartments before they were completed , fueling a debt-driven cycle of rapid growth. Homebuyers of one project in Tianjin city near Beijing previously told CNBC they were waiting years for the units they bought ahead of completion.
The latest S&P forecast also compared the depth of China's real estate downturn so far to how housing crises in Japan, the U.S. and Spain played out in recent decades.
Of the different factors that helped stabilize each of those market slumps, China is working on two: reducing supply and corporate deleveraging, the report said. "China's supply contraction is occurring much earlier and with greater magnitude" than Japan's housing crisis from 1991 to 2014, S&P said.
On the price front, China's residential prices have already fallen by 22% since a 2021 peak, compared with a 67% drop in Japan's after a far greater run-up in prices, the S&P report said.
By comparison, it said the U.S. real estate slump around the financial crisis saw a 26% drop in residential prices.
China's efforts to subsidize mortgages along with wealth effects from the artificial intelligence boom are also helping lift property demand.
Also on Thursday, Guotai Junan International's Chief Economist Hao Zhou published a report predicting the fourth quarter of this year could see the first growth in existing home prices for large, or "tier-one" cities, since the 2021 to 2023 slump.
He noted that since March, tier one cities were more likely than smaller cities to record flat or rising prices. In particular, he said existing home prices in Shanghai have narrowed their year-on-year decline, while those of Beijing have stabilized, rising by 1.4% from a low in January.
Hangzhou, home to DeepSeek and Alibaba , stood out with a record high in its new home sales index, while prices for new homes are only 14.2% below their peak and have fallen less than in most cities, Zhou said.
"The next three months are a key window," he said. "If Shanghai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou avoid a monthly decline through the November 2026 data, this rebound will have outlasted the 2024–25 episode. However, it's still uncertain whether demand will remain sustainable longer term.

Figure caption, Why the British consulate in Jerusalem is now a UK Mission
By Adam Goldsmith   and   James Landale ,  Diplomatic correspondent
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing" and will operate as a "UK Mission".
"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, and stressed the mission would continue "our work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law.
The new steps appear to prevent the diplomatic row between two allies from escalating further.
The British consulate, which was founded in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel and is not affected.
Israel's foreign minister said it had implemented the order to shut the consulate within 30 days, which was one of a series of measures announced on 8 September in response to the UK's sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," Saar posted on X.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering the building.
Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel".
But he acknowledged that the building was "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate from there.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had reported earlier this week that the UK was threatening to expel Israeli diplomats from London.
This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means - for the moment - the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations.
Israel can claim that the British consulate is "closing its operations". A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving Jerusalem.
But Miliband said they were going only temporarily and only for their safety and security.
He also insisted that Israel had no legal right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory," the foreign secretary wrote in a statement.
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building would "not be closing" and would be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem.
However, Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.
"We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence, and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible."
He said the seven UK diplomats remaining in Jerusalem would be "independent and operational" and would "continue to deliver vital services and our work with the Palestinian people".
Image caption, The UK's diplomatic mission in Jerusalem will remain open but at a smaller scale, and with a new name
Asked by the BBC's Today programme if this was a political fudge, UK Foreign Office Minister Stephen Doughty said: "You can see what's changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains".
He added that the "policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with" would continue.
British officials are confident the newly-named UK Mission, Jerusalem remains a diplomatic premise formally protected by the provisions of the Vienna Convention.
The remaining diplomats, they say, will retain the existing privileges and immunities the consul general enjoyed. They are accredited with the Israeli authorities as before and will have the same ability to work and travel in the same way as before, they add.
The mission will continue to provide a wide range of services albeit with a smaller team. That involves supporting British nationals and engaging with Palestinian people and institutions. But since the deal was agreed only on Wednesday night, a lot of detail remained to be worked out.
Sources described the deal as a "political success" because the UK had not backed down on its sanctions on illegal settlements, it had maintained a diplomatic presence in East Jerusalem, and it had avoided a dangerous tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats from London and Tel Aviv. The UK Mission will also - crucially - remain entirely separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv.
Officials also said the fact British diplomats remain on the ground will reinforce the principle that international representation should continue in East Jerusalem.
It was British officials who removed the sign from the consulate. The diplomats who left have gone to other locations in the region to continue their work from there.
It now seems clear the disagreement has been parked until after the Israeli elections at the end of the month.
The UK side wanted to avoid the dispute being "instrumentalized" by any political party during the campaign. But it says negotiations will continue in coming months and the threat of British retaliation remains firmly on the table.

Microsoft starts taking preorders for $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra
Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra contains an Nvidia chip that can run large AI models without generating cloud bills.
The device contains a magnetic USB-C port similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector.
Microsoft also said that Meta will introduce its Muse AI agent for Windows.
Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post .
While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud.
Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics.
"Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement.
Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT.
Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey .
This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices.
In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said.
Microsoft Windows Surface Laptop Ultra and Surface RTX Spark Dev Box
The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event.
A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access.
Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software.
Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving.
"I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true."

Gold edges up after hitting 2-month low as markets weigh Fed rate path
Gold prices edged higher on Thursday as the dollar eased from an 18-month peak, helping bullion recover from a two-month low, while traders weighed the prospect of another US Federal Reserve rate hike this year.
Gold prices ​edged up on Thursday ​after hitting a two-month ​low in the previous session, as investors assessed the minutes of the US Federal Reserve's September meeting for clues on its interest rate trajectory.
Spot gold ⁠rose ‌0.3% to $4,122.99 per ounce by 0916 GMT, having ⁠touched its lowest level since August 5 on Wednesday as a firmer dollar and higher US Treasury yields weighed.
US gold futures for December delivery added 0.18% to $4,147.90.
Fed ‌policymakers were divided last month over the rationale for raising rates, with "some participants" seeing a hike as needed to keep the ​impact of energy and other price shocks at bay, but a more hawkish core viewing it as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation, theminutes showed.
Traders see only a 21.6% ⁠chance of an October rate hike, but are pricing in an 85% probability of ‌an increase in December, according to the CME's ‌FedWatch tool.
"Prices are wobbling above $4,100 as geopolitics stoke inflation fears and year-end Fed hike bets," said Lukman Otunuga, senior research ⁠analyst at FXTM, adding that a stronger dollar and Treasury yields ⁠could weigh further on gold.
"The technical picture adds to ⁠the downside risk. A sustained break below $4,100 opens a path toward $4,000, while a hold above it could trigger a rebound ​toward $4,200."
On the geopolitical front, the ‌number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to the lowest in more than two months after attacks on tankers in the key waterway reached their highest last week since the start of the Middle East war, shipping data ​showed.

A sign displays the prices of unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel as a driver refuels a vehicle at a G&M gas station in Torrance, California, US, on September 28, 2026.
Oil prices climbed Thursday on continued worries about global supply following a record number of tanker attacks that sent crossings through the Strait of Hormuz to a two-month low.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose more than 5% at one point before pulling back to trade 4.8% higher at $105 a barrel at 8.30 a.m. ET . West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, increased by a similar margin to $92.48 a barrel.
Just seven tankers transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, less than half the seven-day average and the lowest number since July 23, preliminary data from Kpler showed. These figures are at times revised higher after ships have moved through the strait, as many switch off their identification systems to try to avoid detection.
Despite the rising number of so-called “dark” transits, there have been a record number of attacks on commercial vessels, with 10 tankers struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, well above the previous weekly high of six, Kpler said in a report Thursday.
The rise in attacks comes even as more crude has been flowing out of the Gulf , highlighting the ongoing risks to crew and cargoes. In the latest attack Wednesday, a tanker reported being struck by “multiple projectiles,” causing casualties, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said.
“There is a clear tug-of-war at the moment between improving supply from the region and lingering threats to supply,” commodities strategists at ING, a bank, wrote in a note Wednesday. “The only way to see prices trade sustainably lower is for lingering risks to be addressed,” they added.
Upward pressure on oil prices also came from concerns about further supply losses as Hurricane Isais heads towards America’s refining hub on the Gulf Coast. Oil majors Shell and Chevron said they would curtail production in the region and evacuate nonessential personnel.
The Shell Norco petroleum refinery and the Valero St. Charles oil refinery are seen in Norco, Louisiana, on April 2, 2026.
A major hurricane could cripple US refining when the world can least afford it
Rising oil prices were accompanied by an increase in European natural gas and diesel prices, fanning inflation fears and contributing to a renewed selloff in European bonds given the continent’s reliance on imported energy.
European benchmark natural gas prices neared their recent high from mid-September earlier on Thursday before pulling back. ICE Gasoil Futures, a benchmark for European diesel prices, closed 6% higher on Wednesday after the International Energy Agency said member governments would not add to the 400 million barrels of oil they agreed to release in March.
To date, roughly 325 million barrels of oil have been released, with approximately 100 million more barrels still to be brought to the market, the IEA said in a statement Wednesday, pledging to “accelerate” those releases. Those 100 million barrels would include the diesel release that G7 countries agreed to last week .
“IEA Member governments still have significant levels of publicly held emergency oil stocks – equivalent to around 1.1 billion barrels, including over 200 million barrels of diesel,” the Paris-based energy body said.
“The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required.”
Average US diesel prices at gas stations were slightly lower on Thursday than the day before, at $6.28 a gallon. Average US regular gasoline prices were flat on the previous day at $4.36 a gallon, according to AAA data.
