U.S. equities pulled back in early trading on Thursday as a combination of surging oil prices and multi-decade high Treasury yields revived Wall Street's concerns over persistent inflation.
After closing at record highs earlier in the week, the major indexes reversed course . The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.5%, the S&P 500 declined 0.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.2% , shedding roughly 105 points shortly after the opening bell.
The market slide reflects a growing tug-of-war between optimistic corporate earnings data and rapidly tightening financial conditions driven by energy costs and borrowing rates.
Energy prices placed heavy downward pressure on equities Thursday morning following reports of escalating hostilities in the Middle East.
Brent crude futures jumped 4% to trade around $104 per barrel , while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) advanced 4% to approximately $92 per barrel . The spike comes amid reports that the U.S. is considering large-scale military operations and potential strikes in Iran ahead of the midterm elections . Supply concerns were further exacerbated by Gulf of Mexico oil producers cutting back production in response to an active tropical storm system.
Iran-aligned Houthi fighters pose next to a captured vehicle following what the source described as an attack on Saudi-backed forces in the location given by the source as al Jawf governorate, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from a video released by Houthi Military Media on September 15, 2026. Photo: HOUTHI MILITARY MEDIA/Handout via REUTERS
Rising oil prices have historically acted as a drag on the broader economy , sparking fears that increased energy costs will keep inflation elevated and force the Federal Reserve to maintain an aggressive monetary policy.
Markets remained on edge as a global bond sell-off continued , pushing borrowing costs to levels not seen in decades. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield hovered near 5.3% , while the 30-year yield climbed to 5.7% . The policy-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield also advanced, gaining more than 3 basis points to reach 4.8%.
FILE - Federal Reserve Board Governor Christopher Waller speaks prior to giving a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker interview in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 3, 2026. Photo: REUTERS/Kylie Cooper
The elevated yields align with fresh hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve. Speaking at a conference in Turkey on Thursday, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned that the central bank’s fight against inflation is not over.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal," Waller stated. "The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Despite the macroeconomic headwinds, underlying U.S. economic data and corporate performance remain resilient.
The Labor Department reported Thursday that initial jobless claims fell to 197,000 for the week ending October 3 , signaling that corporate layoffs remain low and the labor market is holding strong.
On the corporate front, investors are digesting the start of the third-quarter earnings season. PepsiCo (PEP) shares rose 2% after the beverage giant reported adjusted earnings of $2.34 per share on $25.27 billion in revenue , beating Wall Street's expectations, though the company slightly lowered its future profit outlook to stabilize its North American business.
FILE - Plastic bottles of Pepsi are displayed at a grocery store in New York on Nov. 15, 2023. Photo: AP/Ted Shaffrey
Meanwhile, Palantir Technologies (PLTR) emerged as one of the few tech bright spots, jumping more than 3% following an upgrade from Goldman Sachs. The investment bank raised Palantir's price target to $230 , citing a "step function change" in the company's total addressable market driven by sovereign AI contracts.

items.title: Trump's former defense secretary sees no end in sight for Iran war — to the benefit of America's 'greatest adversary' - CNBC
items.summary: Trump's former defense secretary sees no end in sight for Iran war — to the benefit of America's 'greatest adversary'</
items.content:
Ex-U.S. defense secretary Esper: No end in sight for the Iran war
The U.S.-Iran war could stretch on for years, according to ex-U.S. defense secretary Mark Esper.
Esper told CNBC that focus on the Middle East was distracting away from efforts to curb Chinese power and influence.
He labeled China the United States’ “greatest adversary.”
President Donald Trump listens to Secretary of Defense Mark Esper address the daily White House coronavirus response briefing with members of the administration's coronavirus task force at the White House in Washington, March 18, 2020.
The U.S.-Iran war could drag on for years, putting America at risk of overlooking China's rise to power, according to President Donald Trump's former defense secretary.
During a panel discussion at LSEG and Eurasia Group's GZERO Summit in London, Mark Esper said on Thursday he saw the conflict continuing "well into 2027," with a possibility that it could be handed to the next U.S. administration in three years' time.
"At some point, we will reach a point where maybe both sides are willing to come to the table and find a negotiated settlement, but the challenge for president Trump will be he's going to have to get a deal that returns the Strait of Hormuz to the status quo, which is going to be really hard, and is a deal that's better than what [former President Barack Obama] got out of the JCPOA , and I think that's going to be very difficult too," he said.
"So the question is, will he be willing to make that deal and live with the consequences or how the critics judge that deal? And so you can see another path where it gets handed off to the next administration in 2029."
Speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of the event, Esper said he does not see an end to the war "in the foreseeable future."
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) servicemen stand in front of an Iranian national flag at Iran's first military training base for ''self-sacrificing'' forces in southern Tehran, Iran, on September 24, 2026.
"I think it continues at this type of pace where we see the American blockade continue, we see occasional outbursts from either side, and it drags along," he said.
The war, now in its eighth month, has reached an impasse, with Trump saying Wednesday that making a deal with Tehran "isn't really something that I want to do." According to reports , U.S. officials are considering a resumption of large-scale military operations in the coming weeks.
Esper, who served as U.S. Secretary of Defense during Trump's first presidential term from July 2019 to November 2020, said he had long been an advocate for "the economic strangulation" of Iran. But he said such a policy was vulnerable to impatience in Washington.
"The challenge is that policy requires time, discipline and patience, and those aren't things that the states are typically good at doing," he said. "So, if allowed to, I think it could have an impact. It doesn't mean it'll actually bring them back to the table, which would be my end, but it's the least worst option at this point in time."
Over the summer, Trump announced an intensification of sanctions and economic restrictions on Iran, a strategy he labeled "Economic D-Day." The administration has since touted the success of its economic warfare strategies.
A White House official told CNBC Thursday that the U.S. was in "a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing."
"Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways; the easy way or the hard way," they said.
"President Trump will not be played by the Iranian regime," the official added. "The President is satisfied letting the inevitable Iranian collapse play out."
But Esper warned Thursday that with attention in Washington focused on the Iran war, America's "greatest adversary" was building up its capabilities.
"China is our greatest adversary," he said. "It's the lurking threat out there that we're not paying attention to because we're so focused, and have been for 20 plus years now, on the Middle East, and Europe is focused on Russia."
Beijing, he said, was continuing to build economic, technological and diplomatic power, having executed "the largest military buildup in history."
"We're just not paying enough attention to the Chinese," Esper told CNBC. "They've told us by 2049 they want to dominate the Indo-Pacific region and the world for all intents and purposes. They want to be able to call the shots and dictate global governance."
China had been working to this end for at least 30 years, he said.
"Certainly, since their entry into the WTO, they've used the world trading system against us to build their own economic and military power, and they have a game plan," Esper said.
He highlighted Beijing's domination of certain industries and goods, such as electric vehicles, rare earths, solar panels and critical materials. This, he said, had been achieved thanks to the Chinese government's ability to "consolidate control" and direct the country's economy in a certain direction.
"They have a game plan, and they're and they're executing it," Esper said.
"I would focus our efforts on China, and I would do it in partnership with our European and Asian allies, and that would include not just military [alliances], but diplomatic, economic and technological as well."
CNBC reached out to the Chinese government for comment.

Italian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballot
Parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representation
A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament.
Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power.
The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against.
There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced.
Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation.
Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election.
Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy , had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis.
While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme.
Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media.
Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party , said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May.
According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

items.title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11 - TechCrunch
items.summary: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11  TechCrunch
items.content:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city's Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)
Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.
The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called "Execution Containers." This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.
Nadella explained: "One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn't do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space."
He added that Microsoft is enabling that "not just for our apps but apps for anyone's agent. That's what the Windows platform is all about going forward."
The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.
Microsoft wasn't the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It's available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

items.content:
Iran says Strait of Hormuz could reopen within a week as Tehran weighs US response
Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran said.
Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, addresses the media at a press conference during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 25, 2026.
Tehran is still reviewing Washington's response to its proposal, under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days, and could reply within days, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday, according to Iranian semi-official Tasnim news agency.
"The diplomatic process is still continuing," Araghchi said.
Tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to get critical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issued new warnings it would block routes that it has not authorized, sources said.
Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the key waterway since the Iran war began - cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters.
It was part of a plan agreed by both Iran's political leaders and its Revolutionary Guards, the official added.
Vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of the port city of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran on September 5, 2026; illustrative (credit: ATTA KENARE / AFP via Getty Images)
'Iran has no intention of allowing control to slip from its hands'
"Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands, and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil," a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Tehran told Reuters separately.
"This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away," the diplomat added. "It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats," he said.
In recent months, Gulf oil producers have rushed shipments of oil through channels that hug the Omani side of the strait before transferring the oil in open waters in the Gulf of Oman with aerial support from the US, sources have told Reuters.
In the latest incident in the past 24 hours, projectiles struck a tanker some 51 nautical miles off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf, British navy agency UKMTO reported.
Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers had been hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar's Madinat ash Shamal with minor injuries sustained by its crew.
“The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq,” maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global’s subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Thursday.
The vessel's operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment.
"The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait," said Jakob Larsen, chief ​safety & security officer at shipping association BIMCO.

Several pro-Houthi men take part in a rally to recruit new fighters for the group in Sanaa on Wednesday. Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images
Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen
Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen , approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.
The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen , Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.
Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.
A Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz. Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/Reuters Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.
The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week.
Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.
The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.
Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.

items.title: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds
items.summary: Bassam al-Hassan is being sheltered in return for information - including about abducted US reporter Austin Tice.
items.content:
Image caption, Bassam al-Hassan is wanted for crimes against humanity during Syria's Assad regime
A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity , external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.
Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.
An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.
Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation , with Hassan in the chain of command.
Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.
We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.
In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.
"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."
Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.
As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.
Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.
Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.
Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.
One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".
Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.
The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.
Image source, Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images
Image caption, US journalist Austin Tice has been missing since 2012 - Bassam al-Hassan is believed to have been involved in his disappearance
Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran.
A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place - involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran - to bring Hassan to Lebanon.
The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran - secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in.
Image caption, The aftermath of the 2013 chemical attacks in Ghouta, Syria - Bassam al-Hassan is alleged to have shared responsibility
Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.
There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.
Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.
They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".
Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

items.summary: U.S. Treasury yields climbed higher on Thursday as investors eagerly awaited the long-dated bond auction later in the day, after strong sales of 10-year notes.
items.content:
U.S. Treasury yields: investors await 30-year bond auction
Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 28, 2026.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury was higher on Thursday as traders digested comments from a top Federal Reserve official while awaiting another long-dated bond auction.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was more than 2 basis points at 5.299% after reaching its highest level since 2002 in the prior trading day. The 30-year Treasury bond yield was down less than 1 basis point at 5.654% after trading just below a 24-year high on Wednesday. The 2-year Treasury note yield rose more than 4 basis points to 4.812%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that more hikes are needed to bring inflation down after around 5-and-a-half years above the central bank's 2% target, but suggested rates did not need to rise immediately.
"The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings," Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul.
"But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
His comments come a day after minutes from the central bank's September meeting officials expect they will raise interest rates again before the end of the year to head off inflation.
Investors expect that the Fed will keep rates on hold at its next meeting on Oct. 28 and pull the trigger on a hike on Dec. 9.
Investors are looking ahead to the third Treasury auction this week, taking place after midday. On Wednesday, the Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes, with global central banks making up over 80% of the auction, above the auction average of 72.4%.
The department sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday, and is set to sell $22 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday.
"The 10-year auction has set the tone for the Treasury market – at least for the moment," BMO Capital Markets' Ian Lyngen said in a note late Wednesday.
"While the magnitude of the selloff between the September reopening and today's auction might typically have been a reason to keep bidders on the sidelines, we take solace from the sponsorship even as it was the highest-yielding 10-year auction since November 2000."
Lyngen added that Thursday's long-bond auction will be "the next barometer of demand for US debt in an environment of global deficit angst."
Investors also digested the latest weekly jobless claims data, which came in below expectations. For the week ended Oct. 3, initial claims stood at 197,000, marking a decrease of 2,000 from the prior period and lower than the 200,000 that economists polled by Dow Jones were calling for.

items.title: Is the Buffett Indicator Flashing a Warning Sign to Stock Market Investors? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Is the Buffett Indicator Flashing a Warning Sign to Stock Market Investors?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
A popular valuation metric -- known as the Buffett indicator -- measures total U.S. stock market capitalization relative to domestic GDP. It currently sit at 236%, which is essentially its highest level ever. This suggests that U.S. stocks are extremely overvalued.
Is this data point flashing a warning sign to stock market investors?
In the past decade, the S&P 500 index ( ^GSPC -0.39% ) has produced a total return of 324% (as of Oct. 5). On an annualized basis, the 15.5% gain is significantly higher than the benchmark's historical 10% average .
It makes sense why some investors may be worried about the market's valuation these days. The Buffett indicator might hint at poor investment returns in the years ahead.
Investors should take the time to know this metric's limitations, though. It doesn't factor in foreign revenue generated by U.S. companies. Some of the largest technology enterprises , which have a huge weighting in the S&P 500 index, make a lot of money internationally. This artificially inflates the Buffett indicator's numerator.
The money supply has also ballooned in the past 10 years. That's a tailwind for equities since it results in more liquidity entering the financial system that can flow to stocks.
The takeaway for investors is to use the Buffett indicator to understand the current state of markets. But don't expect this to be a tool that helps you time your buy and sell decisions. Nothing beats putting money to work early and letting compounding take over.

items.summary: 3 Glorious Growth Stocks to Buy Hand Over Fist if the Stock Market Crashes  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 stock market index has more than doubled from its 2022 bear market low point, driven by the technology sector, which has produced particularly strong returns thanks to the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom. However, a rising inflation rate, interest rate hikes, and even a potential slowdown in AI development by labs like Anthropic and OpenAI could derail the current bull market.
The risk of a severe downturn is especially high right now because of the market's elevated valuation. The S&P 500 has a Shiller Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) ratio of 41.4, the second-highest level since the peak of the dot-com internet bubble in 2000. The index plummeted by 49% when that bubble eventually burst, and while I'm not predicting a similar decline this time around, investors might want to use  caution.
Fortunately, the market typically trends higher over the long term, so any severe crash will almost certainly be a buying opportunity. Below, I'm going to share three stocks that investors might want to scoop up at a discount if the broader market tumbles and these stocks dip with it.
Zscaler ( ZS +2.37% ) was one of the early pioneers of the zero-trust cybersecurity architecture, which is now one of the best defenses against increasingly sophisticated AI-powered attacks. Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange starts by protecting the identity layer, treating all network login attempts as hostile. It verifies each user not only by their credentials, but also by their location and the device they are using to ensure it's really them.
Moreover, the Zero Trust Exchange only gives employees access to the applications they need to complete their jobs, so a hacker won't have free rein within the corporate network even if they bypass the identity layer. Zscaler added new tools to the Exchange earlier this year, like AI Broker, which strictly monitors communications between AI agents, and Endpoint AI Security, which protects the computers and devices employees are using to run AI applications.

This is all a part of Zscaler's "Zero Trust Everywhere" philosophy, which is now critical because AI-powered threats are constantly hunting for vulnerabilities in corporate networks. Keeping assets and internal agents hidden behind something like the Exchange has never been more important.
Zscaler generated a record $3.35 billion in revenue during its 2026 fiscal year (ended July 31), a 25% increase from the prior year. Its stock is already attractively valued, so any sell-off during a broader market correction could be a very juicy buying opportunity. With a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 9.3 as I write this, it's far cheaper than rivals like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks .
2. Uber Technologies: A future leader of the autonomous driving revolution
Dozens of companies around the world are developing self-driving cars , but Uber Technologies ( UBER +0.29% ) isn't one of them. Instead, it's partnering with many of those companies and allowing them to deploy their vehicles into its global ride-hailing network.
This is a win-win arrangement. Developers of self-driving cars can immediately access Uber's pool of 208 million monthly active customers, while Uber gets to offer autonomous vehicles without incurring the costs involved in designing or manufacturing them. Plus, Uber paid $25 billion to the human drivers in its network during the second quarter of 2026 (ended June 30), which was its single largest cost, so the shift toward autonomous vehicles will significantly improve the company's financial results.
Like Zscaler, Uber stock is already attractively valued. Based on the company's trailing 12-month revenue of $55.2 billion, its stock is trading at a P/S ratio of just 2.5, making it significantly cheaper than the technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 index, which has a P/S ratio of 6.5. Therefore, Uber looks like a solid investment even today, so any dip in its stock from here could be a great long-term buy.

The average business doesn't have the billions of dollars or technical expertise required to build its own AI data centers. Therefore, many of them choose to rent computing capacity from third-party cloud providers . Amazon and Microsoft dominate this particular industry, but DigitalOcean ( DOCN -0.06% ) is taking the fight to those trillion-dollar giants.
DigitalOcean operates around 20 AI data centers spread across the globe, and they are fitted with specialized chips from suppliers like Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . It rents the computing capacity to businesses through a platform called AI-Native Cloud, which also provides access to the latest foundation models from labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, in addition to over 70 open-source models.

DigitalOcean had $1.1 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) as of June 30. AI customers accounted for $234 million of that total, a whopping 212% increase from the year-ago period. That growth rate could accelerate, because the company's order backlog from customers who were waiting for more data centers to come online was $894 million as of June 30, a staggering 12-fold increase from the same time last year.
DigitalOcean stock is trading at a P/S ratio of 15.7, a steep premium to its five-year average of 7.9, so some of its future growth is already priced in. While I wouldn't buy it at the current price, it could be an enticing long-term buy if it experiences a correction of 20% to 30% in the coming months.

items.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
items.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
items.content:
Figure caption, Moment Margaret Hamilton receives Presidential Medal of Freedom
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.
"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.
It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.
But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
Image caption, Hamilton with the printed computer code in 1969
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.
Image caption, Hamilton being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then President Barack Obama in 2016

items.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
items.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.
items.content:
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.
The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.
"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.
There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 19:00, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.
The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Figure caption, Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.
Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.
And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Image caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.
Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.
To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.
In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Figure caption, Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BFMTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.
Image caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings
The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.
His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.
But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

Broadcom generates about US$59.4b from Semiconductor Solutions and roughly US$29.7b from Infrastructure Software, with a market value near US$1.79t.

The real swing factor is how one shift in high end AI test demand could feed through to pricing power and long term margin strength.

items.title: Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles
items.summary: Saudi Arabia says two of the missiles intercepted were headed towards the capital, Riyadh.
items.content:
Share Saudi-led coalition says it intercepts three Houthi ballistic missiles on social media
Black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after an earlier Houthi attack on September 19, 2026 [File: Reuters]
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government says it has intercepted ballistic missiles allegedly fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
In a statement, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said his forces intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles heading in the direction of the Saudi capital Riyadh, and one missile in the direction of the city of Khamis Mushait, close to the Yemeni border, on Thursday.

Separately, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said in a statement on X that falling debris from an intercepted missile had caused material damage to a kindergarten and medical clinic complex in Riyadh. It did not indicate if there were any casualties.
Yahya Saree, Yemen’s Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-aligned group launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday afternoon, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
Witnesses told The Associated Press news agency that they heard several explosions in Riyadh on Thursday, including one at the city’s airport that halted flights. Al Jazeera could not independently confirm the reports.
In recent days, the Houthis have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating in the kingdom’s airspace, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target for the Houthis.
Following the latest reports, Air India said on Thursday that it had cancelled flights to and from Riyadh until at least the weekend, and the Germany-based Lufthansa ⁠Group ⁠airlines said they were suspending flights to Riyadh through October 16, according to the Reuters news agency.
Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks, claimed by the Houthis on Tuesday and Wednesday. At least three civilians were killed and 36 injured, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the attacks on the two airports, saying in a post on X that they “represent a grave violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to the security of the region and the safety of civilians, civil objects, and air navigation”.
These were not the first Houthi strikes on Saudi airports. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Meanwhile, inside Yemen, explosions have been reported near the airport in the Houthi-controlled Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, according to local sources.
The cause and impact of these explosions are not immediately clear.
Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, reporting from Taiz in Yemen, said intense fighting is raging between armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis in al-Shamayatayn, al-Maafer and the southern and western countryside of Taiz governorate.
“The Houthis are pushing into rural areas that have not seen conflict for years, aiming to open a supply route because their lines towards al-Kadaha and al-Waziiya, which link Aden, Lahij and Taiz, are nearly cut off by advancing government forces”, she said.
Al-Yamani added that pro-government forces are within striking distance of al-Waziiya and the Kahboub Mountains overlooking Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Pro-government forces have reported more than 2,000 operations against the Houthis, and are preparing for a “dangerous escalation”, she said.
Children pause for a photo in a makeshift camp for people displaced by clashes between Iran-aligned Houthi fighters and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, near Aden, Yemen, October 7, 2026 [Reuters] More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to data released by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM described the crisis in a statement on Wednesday as alarming, with displacement figures surging from the 76,000 recorded in mid-September.
